epithet.en: The wife and mother who leaves her husband for Count Vronsky
epithet.da: Hustruen og moderen, der forlader sin mand for grev Vronskij

2.modern-en: Anna's telegram from Petersburg arrives at the Oblonskys': she is coming to Moscow to broker peace in her brother's marriage.

4.modern-en: Anna's coming visit is invoked by Stiva as the household waits on her arrival.

5.modern-en: Anna is named again as the powerful sister-in-law whose visit Moscow is anticipating.

17.modern-en: Anna's brother Stiva and Vronsky wait for her train at the Moscow railway station.

18.modern-en: Anna steps off the train in Moscow; Vronsky catches a first lingering look at her on the platform.

19.modern-en: Anna goes straight up to Dolly's room and begins, gently, to talk her into forgiving Stiva.

20.modern-en: Anna sits with Dolly all afternoon, defending Stiva while admitting his fault, and quietly wins her round.

21.modern-en: Anna brokers the reconciliation between Stiva and Dolly and stays for the evening with the household.

22.modern-en: Anna attends the great Moscow ball; Vronsky's attention to her, in front of Kitty, sets the whole story in motion.

23.modern-en: Anna leaves the ball shaken and that night announces she is going back to Petersburg earlier than planned.

28.modern-en: Anna takes the night train home; on the journey her conversation with Vronsky in the snowstorm crosses every line of decorum.

29.modern-en: Anna is met at the Petersburg station by Karenin and notices for the first time how his big ears irritate her.

30.modern-en: Anna throws herself back into her household, holds Seryozha tightly, and tries to forget Moscow.

31.modern-en: Anna attends a salon evening and is observed by Karenin to be in an excited, unfamiliar mood.

32.modern-en: Anna pretends not to understand Karenin's first guarded remarks about her behaviour.

33.modern-en: Anna goes to Betsy Tverskaya's reception, where Vronsky meets her in plain view of society.

34.modern-en: Anna sits with Vronsky apart from the rest of Betsy's room while the gossip closes around them.

36.modern-en: Anna is referred to in Petersburg drawing rooms as the woman Vronsky is pursuing.

38.modern-en: Anna is the subject of Lidia Ivanovna's pious circle's disapproving talk.

40.modern-en: Anna attends another Tverskaya soirée and lets Vronsky speak to her with new openness.

41.modern-en: Anna receives Karenin's careful letter setting out the conditions of their continued life together.

42.modern-en: Anna deflects Karenin's questions with cold politeness when he tries to talk to her at home.

43.modern-en: Anna goes on receiving Vronsky and ignoring Karenin's reproofs.

44.modern-en: Anna sits at the opera with Vronsky's eyes on her from across the hall.

45.modern-en: Anna gives in to Vronsky in private; the affair becomes a settled fact between them.

52.modern-en: Anna's affair is the talk of Petersburg as Vronsky's regiment carries on as usual.

53.modern-en: Anna is named in the regiment's casual gossip about Vronsky's evenings.

55.modern-en: Anna is invoked in Vronsky's reflections on whether to leave the army for her sake.

56.modern-en: Anna sits with Seryozha for his lessons, conscious that her household has changed around her.

57.modern-en: Anna and Karenin pass each other in their own house with brittle politeness.

58.modern-en: Anna is at the steeplechase; when Vronsky falls she cries out and gives herself away to Karenin and everyone else.

60.modern-en: Anna confesses to Karenin in the carriage on the way home that she loves Vronsky and hates her husband.

61.modern-en: Anna receives Karenin's written ultimatum that she will keep up appearances and give up Vronsky.

62.modern-en: Anna reads Karenin's letter and refuses to abandon Vronsky on any terms.

63.modern-en: Anna goes on receiving Vronsky in defiance of Karenin's rules.

82.modern-en: Anna is reported as living openly between Karenin's house and Vronsky's circle.

83.modern-en: Anna is named in Karenin's ministry circles as the wife about whom everyone is now whispering.

84.modern-en: Anna is reported as pregnant by Vronsky and in a state of growing despair.

85.modern-en: Anna meets Vronsky in stolen evenings and is increasingly worn by her divided life.

86.modern-en: Anna is shown lurching between defiance and dread as the pregnancy becomes undeniable.

87.modern-en: Anna writes Vronsky a despairing note that brings him back to her with new resolve.

88.modern-en: Anna is the subject of Vronsky's conversations with his regiment friends about leaving the service.

89.modern-en: Anna meets Vronsky at Betsy Tverskaya's and tells him she is going to lose herself in scandal soon.

90.modern-en: Anna is named in the talk between Serpuhovskoy and Vronsky about his future.

91.modern-en: Anna receives Vronsky at her own house when Karenin is away; the visit is interrupted by Karenin's return.

92.modern-en: Anna tells Vronsky she is pregnant; Karenin tells her he wants a divorce.

102.modern-en: Anna is in childbed, near death after the birth of Vronsky's daughter.

103.modern-en: Anna, raving with fever, begs Karenin to forgive both her and Vronsky.

104.modern-en: Anna is at the centre of the great forgiveness scene as Karenin grants her absolution and Vronsky weeps in shame.

105.modern-en: Anna recovers and the household, including Lidia Ivanovna, gathers around her.

107.modern-en: Anna is reported as a strange new presence in the Karenin household, half estranged from everyone.

108.modern-en: Anna is at home when Stiva calls to start pressing the case for a divorce.

109.modern-en: Anna stays in the house under Lidia Ivanovna's eye and grows more impatient with her position.

113.modern-en: Anna is mentioned in the lawyer scene as the wife who would need to be exposed to provide grounds.

118.modern-en: Anna is reported by Dolly to be living abroad with Vronsky.

119.modern-en: Anna's life abroad is referred to in Karenin's household as an unspoken disgrace.

120.modern-en: Anna is named in conversation between Dolly and Karenin about what to tell Seryozha.

121.modern-en: Anna is named again as the mother whose name Karenin has banned in the house.

122.modern-en: Anna is referred to in Moscow society as the woman Vronsky has run off with.

123.modern-en: Anna is on Stiva's mind as he settles Levin's wedding details and his sister's situation in turn.

124.modern-en: Anna is referred to in the family gossip Stiva is half hiding from his guests.

129.modern-en: Anna is named in Stiva's after-wedding talk about who is still receiving her in Petersburg.

131.modern-en: Anna is in Italy with Vronsky in the small town where they are taking a palazzo.

132.modern-en: Anna's first months of freedom abroad are described: she is unforgivably happy and afraid of losing Vronsky.

133.modern-en: Anna proposes that the artist Mihailov paint her portrait and meets him in his studio.

134.modern-en: Anna is the model who unsettles the painter Mihailov as he opens his door to her and Vronsky.

135.modern-en: Anna stands before Mihailov's Christ-before-Pilate painting and is moved by the figure of Christ.

136.modern-en: Anna's portrait is begun and the small society of the Italian town orbits around her.

137.modern-en: Anna sits for the portrait and watches Vronsky lose interest in painting; they decide to return to Russia.

145.modern-en: Anna's name dominates the séance circle around Karenin as Lidia Ivanovna works to block her divorce.

147.modern-en: Anna is referred to as the mother whose absence Seryozha is being trained to accept.

148.modern-en: Anna is named again in the séance scene as the wife about whom Landau is supposed to deliver judgement.

149.modern-en: Anna is the silent loser of the verdict that Karenin and Lidia Ivanovna take from Landau's mumbling.

152.modern-en: Anna decides to slip into Karenin's house to see Seryozha on his birthday.

153.modern-en: Anna sneaks past the servants, finds Seryozha asleep, wakes him, and holds him until Karenin walks in.

154.modern-en: Anna is forced to leave the house without saying goodbye; Karenin issues a written ban on further visits.

155.modern-en: Anna receives Yashvin at her Petersburg flat in place of Vronsky and reads, in the change, that something is wrong.

156.modern-en: Anna is in keyed-up high spirits over dinner with Vronsky and Yashvin, almost flirting with Yashvin and Tushkevitch.

157.modern-en: Anna defies Vronsky and goes alone to the opera, where ladies turn their backs on her in plain view.

159.modern-en: Anna is invoked at Pokrovskoe as the sister-in-law Dolly is planning to visit.

164.modern-en: Anna is named again as Dolly prepares to set off for Vozdvizhenskoe.

171.modern-en: Anna is on Dolly's mind as she rides across the country to visit her at Vozdvizhenskoe.

173.modern-en: Anna receives Dolly at Vozdvizhenskoe and shows her the new estate with Vronsky.

174.modern-en: Anna entertains Dolly and Vronsky's guests at a long, smoothly run dinner.

175.modern-en: Anna walks in the garden with Dolly and tells her she will not have more children, only this baby of Vronsky's.

176.modern-en: Anna brings Dolly to see the model hospital Vronsky has built and lays out their plans for the estate.

177.modern-en: Anna plays hostess in the evening, alert to every shift of mood in Vronsky and his guests.

178.modern-en: Anna talks honestly with Dolly about Seryozha, the divorce, and what she has begun to fear about herself.

179.modern-en: Anna sees Dolly off and is left with the sense that her old life will not come back.

180.modern-en: Anna's situation is reflected in Dolly's silent thoughts on the drive home.

181.modern-en: Anna takes her place in Vronsky's household routines again after Dolly's visit.

182.modern-en: Anna is named as the woman waiting for Vronsky at Vozdvizhenskoe as he goes off to the elections.

188.modern-en: Anna sends word to Vronsky during the elections demanding he come back early.

189.modern-en: Anna welcomes Vronsky back from the elections but cannot hide the strain between them.

197.modern-en: Anna is named at the English Club as the woman keeping Vronsky from his evening at the tables.

198.modern-en: Anna is invoked in Stiva's plans for the Petersburg trip he is about to take on her behalf.

199.modern-en: Anna writes to Vronsky from Moscow about Seryozha and the divorce.

200.modern-en: Anna is in Moscow, restless, waiting on Stiva's mission to Karenin in Petersburg.

201.modern-en: Anna meets Levin at her Moscow flat; Levin is, almost against his will, captivated by her.

206.modern-en: Anna waits in Moscow for word of how Stiva's renewed approach to Karenin has gone.

207.modern-en: Anna receives, through Stiva, the news that Karenin will refer the question to Lidia Ivanovna and Landau.

208.modern-en: Anna grows more anxious as the days pass without a clear answer from Petersburg.

211.modern-en: Anna learns through Stiva that Karenin has, on mystical grounds, finally refused her the divorce.

212.modern-en: Anna quarrels with Vronsky over how he handles her despair and accuses him of no longer loving her.

213.modern-en: Anna sends a series of small, increasingly desperate notes to Vronsky to bring him back to her.

214.modern-en: Anna and Vronsky have their worst quarrel; Yashvin walks in mid-argument.

215.modern-en: Anna refuses to go with Vronsky to his mother's place in the country and feels herself going under.

216.modern-en: Anna tries to visit Seryozha, is turned away, and drifts through Moscow in a daze.

217.modern-en: Anna calls at Dolly's and sees Kitty there briefly; the visit confirms her sense of being shut out.

218.modern-en: Anna takes a long carriage ride through Moscow turning Yashvin's line over in her head and rehearsing her grievances.

219.modern-en: Anna travels to the country station thinking of Seryozha, Karenin, and Vronsky, and watches the lamplit platform pass.

220.modern-en: Anna throws herself under the wheels of an oncoming train at a country railway station.

epithet.en: Cavalry officer who abandons his career and engagement for Anna
epithet.da: Kavaleriofficer, der opgiver sin karriere og forlovelse for Anna

11.modern-en: Vronsky is named to Levin by Stiva as the young officer the Shtcherbatskys appear to favour for Kitty.

12.modern-en: Vronsky is the rival Levin is half preparing himself to meet at the Shtcherbatskys' house.

13.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to in the household as the courtship Princess Shtcherbatskaya prefers for Kitty.

14.modern-en: Vronsky is on the women's minds at the Shtcherbatskys' as Kitty refuses Levin.

15.modern-en: Vronsky's expected proposal hangs over the evening Kitty has just spent turning Levin down.

16.modern-en: Vronsky calls at the Shtcherbatskys' for the first time on the page, charming the household.

17.modern-en: Vronsky is at the Moscow station with Stiva when Anna's train comes in from Petersburg.

18.modern-en: Vronsky sees Anna for the first time on the platform and is caught looking at her.

20.modern-en: Vronsky calls at the Oblonskys' to leave a card on Anna and is mentioned in the talk that follows.

21.modern-en: Vronsky is invoked in the dressing-room conversation between Anna and Kitty before the ball.

22.modern-en: Vronsky abandons Kitty at the ball to dance with Anna, the public turning point of the whole novel.

23.modern-en: Vronsky is named in the post-ball talk as the man who has thrown Kitty over for Madame Karenina.

24.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to in passing as the officer whose conduct at the ball is the gossip of Moscow.

28.modern-en: Vronsky takes the same Moscow–Petersburg train as Anna, finds her in the snow at a stop, and tells her he loves her.

29.modern-en: Vronsky is at the Petersburg station as Anna arrives and is conspicuous to Karenin.

30.modern-en: Vronsky calls at the Karenin house with a small pretext and is received with formal politeness.

31.modern-en: Vronsky is named in Lidia Ivanovna's circle as the young officer dangling after Anna.

32.modern-en: Vronsky's presence in Petersburg is referred to as the new strain Karenin is trying to ignore.

33.modern-en: Vronsky meets Anna at Betsy Tverskaya's reception and they fall straight into a long aside.

34.modern-en: Vronsky and Anna sit apart from Betsy's room in plain view; the watch on them tightens.

36.modern-en: Vronsky is on Kitty's mind as she goes through the season trying not to think of him.

37.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to again as the man whose name Kitty cannot bear to hear.

38.modern-en: Vronsky's name is dropped in Lidia Ivanovna's drawing room as a worldly young man of bad influence.

39.modern-en: Vronsky calls at the Tverskaya circle, where he and Anna can talk openly.

40.modern-en: Vronsky's evenings now revolve around Anna's nights out in Petersburg's smart set.

41.modern-en: Vronsky is the man Karenin names, finally, in his cold letter to Anna about decorum.

42.modern-en: Vronsky goes on calling at the salons where he can see Anna, indifferent to Karenin's coolness.

43.modern-en: Vronsky is described as having reorganised his whole regiment life around being near Anna.

44.modern-en: Vronsky is at the opera, his eyes on Anna across the hall.

45.modern-en: Vronsky's affair with Anna becomes consummated and a settled fact.

50.modern-en: Vronsky is named in Stiva's gossip with Levin as the rival who broke Kitty's heart.

51.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to again in Stiva and Levin's argument about how women are won and lost.

52.modern-en: Vronsky is shown at the regiment in his easy, gambling, soldierly life, with Anna at its centre.

53.modern-en: Vronsky is in the regiment dining room when Captain Yashvin arrives; he is named as Anna's lover.

54.modern-en: Vronsky drags Petritsky out of bed with Yashvin in preparation for the steeplechase.

55.modern-en: Vronsky takes a long ride out to look over his mare Frou-Frou before the race.

56.modern-en: Vronsky drives out to Anna's country house and is met there in secret.

57.modern-en: Vronsky and Anna talk about her pregnancy, which they both now suspect.

58.modern-en: Vronsky rides Frou-Frou in the great steeplechase before the Tsar and falls catastrophically at the last ditch.

59.modern-en: Vronsky, dazed and devastated by Frou-Frou's broken back, is led off by Yashvin and walks home in shock.

60.modern-en: Vronsky is the man Anna names in the carriage when she confesses to Karenin she loves him.

61.modern-en: Vronsky is named in Karenin's drafted ultimatum to Anna.

62.modern-en: Vronsky is the man Anna will not give up, as her response to Karenin makes plain.

63.modern-en: Vronsky goes on seeing Anna in defiance of Karenin's rules.

79.modern-en: Vronsky is mentioned as the lover whose existence is keeping Levin from his work at Pokrovskoe.

82.modern-en: Vronsky is named in the Petersburg gossip the regiment passes around about Anna's affair.

84.modern-en: Vronsky is described as the central problem in Karenin's life as he considers what to do about Anna's pregnancy.

85.modern-en: Vronsky is increasingly absent from the regiment as Anna's situation worsens.

86.modern-en: Vronsky is the man Anna writes desperate notes to as Karenin tightens his rules.

88.modern-en: Vronsky is at the regiment hearing Yashvin and Venovsky settle his gambling debts.

89.modern-en: Vronsky is in Betsy Tverskaya's drawing room when Anna tells him she cannot go on like this.

90.modern-en: Vronsky meets Serpuhovskoy and is offered the army future he is about to walk away from.

91.modern-en: Vronsky borrows Yashvin's hired fly to slip across Petersburg to Anna and is caught by Karenin's return.

102.modern-en: Vronsky learns that Anna is in childbed and may die; he goes to the Karenin house and meets her husband.

103.modern-en: Vronsky stands in Anna's sickroom and is forgiven by Karenin in the same breath as Anna.

104.modern-en: Vronsky, undone by Karenin's forgiveness, tries to shoot himself in his own apartment and survives.

105.modern-en: Vronsky is reported as recovering from his self-inflicted wound.

108.modern-en: Vronsky resigns his commission and prepares to take Anna abroad.

109.modern-en: Vronsky is mentioned in Stiva's negotiations with Karenin as the man Anna intends to live with.

110.modern-en: Vronsky and Anna leave Petersburg for Italy, abandoning his career and her marriage.

118.modern-en: Vronsky's name comes up in Dolly's account of Anna's life abroad.

119.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to in Petersburg society as Anna's lover living openly with her in Europe.

120.modern-en: Vronsky is invoked in Karenin's household as the man whose name Seryozha is not to hear.

121.modern-en: Vronsky is mentioned in Dolly's appeals to Karenin as the father of Anna's new child.

123.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to in Moscow gossip on the eve of Levin's wedding.

124.modern-en: Vronsky is named in the family talk about who has and has not been invited to the Levin wedding.

126.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to in passing at the wedding as the source of the family's old wound.

131.modern-en: Vronsky is in Italy with Anna, runs into Golenishtchev, and decides to take a palazzo and paint.

132.modern-en: Vronsky is described as outwardly content with Anna and inwardly bored by the freedom he has chosen.

133.modern-en: Vronsky reads of the painter Mihailov and proposes that Anna sit for him as a small philanthropy.

134.modern-en: Vronsky brings Anna and Golenishtchev to Mihailov's studio and is taken by the painter's picture.

135.modern-en: Vronsky talks technique with Mihailov in front of the Christ-and-Pilate picture and is gently corrected.

136.modern-en: Vronsky buys Mihailov's small boys-fishing painting and continues to dabble at his own work.

137.modern-en: Vronsky drops painting again, and he and Anna decide to leave Italy and return to Russia.

147.modern-en: Vronsky's name is invoked again in Lidia Ivanovna's circle as the seducer who took Anna away.

148.modern-en: Vronsky is named once more in the séance scene as the man for whom Anna ruined her marriage.

152.modern-en: Vronsky is back in Petersburg with Anna in temporary quarters as she plans her visit to Seryozha.

153.modern-en: Vronsky waits while Anna goes alone to see Seryozha at his father's house.

155.modern-en: Vronsky returns to Anna's Petersburg flat with Yashvin in tow instead of coming alone.

156.modern-en: Vronsky watches Anna's edgy mood through dinner and Yashvin's evening with them.

157.modern-en: Vronsky tries to stop Anna from going to the opera alone; she goes anyway, and the ladies turn their backs.

159.modern-en: Vronsky is named at Pokrovskoe in the household talk about Anna's situation.

164.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to again as Dolly prepares to leave for Vozdvizhenskoe.

173.modern-en: Vronsky receives Dolly at Vozdvizhenskoe with a measured, manorial courtesy.

174.modern-en: Vronsky presides at the long Vozdvizhenskoe dinner with his hand-picked guests.

175.modern-en: Vronsky's running of the estate and the hospital is the subject he most enjoys showing Dolly.

177.modern-en: Vronsky watches Anna through the evening, alert to every shift in her temper.

178.modern-en: Vronsky is named again in Anna's frank talk with Dolly about why she cannot ask for the divorce herself.

179.modern-en: Vronsky sees Dolly off civilly the morning of her departure.

180.modern-en: Vronsky is invoked in Dolly's thoughts as the man who has built Anna a small kingdom and lost her freedom in it.

181.modern-en: Vronsky goes back to running the estate after Dolly leaves, with Anna's mood deepening behind him.

182.modern-en: Vronsky is named as the host whose guests Levin meets briefly when the gentry pass through.

186.modern-en: Vronsky stops in at the elections to lend his name to the modernising party.

187.modern-en: Vronsky leaves the elections at Anna's summons and returns to Vozdvizhenskoe.

188.modern-en: Vronsky finds Anna more anxious than before he left for the elections.

189.modern-en: Vronsky goes back to working the estate while Anna grows more demanding.

190.modern-en: Vronsky is in Moscow with Anna at her flat for the winter.

196.modern-en: Vronsky greets Levin at the English Club and brings him out of the gambling rooms.

197.modern-en: Vronsky takes Levin upstairs to dine and watches over Yashvin's play.

198.modern-en: Vronsky brings Levin from the club to Anna's flat to introduce them.

199.modern-en: Vronsky watches Levin meet Anna and senses she has caught his sympathy.

200.modern-en: Vronsky is in Moscow as Stiva sets out for Petersburg with Anna's renewed divorce appeal.

201.modern-en: Vronsky goes to the club with Stiva while Anna stays home waiting on news.

209.modern-en: Vronsky is named in the séance circle as the lover for whom Karenin will not surrender the marriage.

212.modern-en: Vronsky quarrels with Anna over how to manage her disappointment about the divorce.

213.modern-en: Vronsky reads Anna's stream of desperate notes between his other Moscow engagements.

214.modern-en: Vronsky has his worst quarrel with Anna; Yashvin walks in mid-argument.

215.modern-en: Vronsky refuses to put off his trip to his mother's, even as Anna falls apart.

216.modern-en: Vronsky leaves the house in the morning convinced he is in the right; Anna is left to her own thoughts.

217.modern-en: Vronsky goes to his mother's country place by train, unaware of how far gone Anna is.

218.modern-en: Vronsky reads Anna's last notes at the station and only half registers what they say.

219.modern-en: Vronsky writes a reply too late and is not at the train station when Anna is.

220.modern-en: Vronsky is at his mother's house when the news reaches him that Anna has thrown herself under a train.

222.modern-en: Vronsky is described in mourning, half deranged by Anna's death and his own toothache, withdrawn from everyone.

224.modern-en: Vronsky boards the train for the Serbian war with Yashvin, leaving Russia and the small daughter behind.

225.modern-en: Vronsky is seen off at the station by Sergey Ivanovitch and others on his way to Serbia.

235.modern-en: Vronsky is referred to as the lost figure who has gone to Serbia, never to be heard from inside the novel again.

epithet.en: Anna's husband, a senior government minister

5.modern-en: Karenin is named as the senior brother-in-law through whom Stiva keeps his lucrative Moscow post.

17.modern-en: Karenin is referred to in Vronsky's regiment as a Petersburg dignitary; Anna's married life is sketched.

20.modern-en: Karenin meets Anna at the Petersburg railway station; she notices for the first time how unattractive his big ears look.

29.modern-en: Karenin observes the change in Anna after her Moscow trip but cannot bring himself to name what he is seeing.

31.modern-en: Karenin attends a Petersburg salon evening and notes Anna's animated mood without confronting it.

32.modern-en: Karenin sits up writing late, mechanically rehearsing what he will say to Anna about Vronsky.

33.modern-en: Karenin has his first careful conversation with Anna about appearances; she rebuffs him with mock incomprehension.

38.modern-en: Karenin continues his ministry routine while ladies' gossip about Anna circulates around Petersburg.

40.modern-en: Karenin attends a Tverskaya soirée and watches Anna and Vronsky from a distance.

41.modern-en: Karenin writes a stiff letter to Anna setting out the terms on which their married life may continue.

42.modern-en: Karenin returns from his ministry and finds Anna evasive about her movements.

43.modern-en: Karenin grows more suspicious; he sketches a sermon-like reproof in his head.

44.modern-en: Karenin watches Anna at the opera and sees Vronsky's eyes follow her every move.

45.modern-en: Karenin presses Anna for an explanation, and she gives him a chilly, untrue one.

52.modern-en: Karenin throws himself into his Polish-question report, treating Anna's behaviour as a problem of administration.

55.modern-en: Karenin is referred to in passing as the husband Vronsky's regiment friends quietly pity.

56.modern-en: Karenin allows Seryozha's lesson to run, listens to Anna read, and keeps up the household routine.

57.modern-en: Karenin's measured politeness with Anna grows steelier as the talk in town reaches his ministry colleagues.

58.modern-en: Karenin attends the steeplechase and watches Anna's face go bone-white when Vronsky falls.

60.modern-en: Karenin confronts Anna directly in the carriage on the way home; she admits that she loves Vronsky.

61.modern-en: Karenin lies awake formulating his official response: a refusal of divorce and a demand for outward decorum.

62.modern-en: Karenin sends Anna his ruling in writing — they will keep up appearances, and she will give up Vronsky.

63.modern-en: Karenin works at his despatches, deliberately not asking after Anna, while his decision settles into law in his own house.

82.modern-en: Karenin is mentioned among the Petersburg dignitaries Vronsky's set quietly mocks.

83.modern-en: Karenin pushes his commission's report through, banking his career against his domestic disaster.

84.modern-en: Karenin learns Anna has gone to the country with Vronsky and rehearses the legal forms of disgrace.

85.modern-en: Karenin keeps Petersburg society at arm's length and lets his work absorb him.

86.modern-en: Karenin's ministry rivals scent weakness and begin to mobilise against him.

87.modern-en: Karenin's outward composure cracks in private; he weeps once and then files the moment away.

91.modern-en: Karenin learns that Anna is pregnant, and that the child is not his.

92.modern-en: Karenin tells Anna in a single icy meeting that he intends to seek a divorce.

102.modern-en: Karenin is called home from Moscow because Anna is in childbed and may not survive.

103.modern-en: Karenin sits at Anna's bedside; she begs his forgiveness through the haze of fever.

104.modern-en: Karenin, in the most religious moment of his life, forgives Anna and Vronsky and resolves to keep her in the house.

105.modern-en: Karenin shows the new baby to Anna and arranges for Lidia Ivanovna to take charge of the household.

106.modern-en: Karenin discovers, as Anna recovers, that his forgiveness has not made her love him.

107.modern-en: Karenin tries, awkwardly, to live as Anna's husband again, while the Petersburg world watches.

108.modern-en: Karenin endures Vronsky's visit and the impossibility of the situation begins to wear on him.

109.modern-en: Karenin lets Lidia Ivanovna run the house and shield him from Anna's continued unhappiness.

110.modern-en: Karenin's official position grows more fragile as the scandal seeps into Petersburg gossip.

111.modern-en: Karenin reluctantly agrees, at Stiva's pressing, to consider releasing Anna from the marriage.

113.modern-en: Karenin meets a lawyer about divorce procedure and recoils from what it would require.

114.modern-en: Karenin retreats from the divorce plan and tells Anna she may continue living abroad on his terms.

118.modern-en: Karenin is reported by Dolly to be living in austere bachelor isolation, governed by Lidia Ivanovna.

119.modern-en: Karenin's ministry standing slips further; he holds onto his rank by sheer correctness.

120.modern-en: Karenin allows Dolly to see Seryozha during her visit but refuses to relax his rules.

121.modern-en: Karenin politely refuses Dolly's plea that Anna be allowed to write to or see Seryozha.

123.modern-en: Karenin works late at his despatches as his official influence quietly drains away.

124.modern-en: Karenin is observed at a Petersburg gathering, smiled at and ignored in equal measure.

36.modern-en: Levin is referred to by Princess Shtcherbatskaya as the suitor Kitty turned away.

75.modern-en: Levin sits with Sergey Ivanovitch and argues over the district council and the value of public service.

76.modern-en: Levin invites Dolly to bring the children to Pokrovskoe and helps her with the leaky country house.

93.modern-en: Levin sets out to visit Sviazhsky's estate and meets the model landowners along the way.

99.modern-en: Levin is interrupted by the arrival of his brother Nikolay, more skeletal than before.

101.modern-en: Levin sees Nikolay off with strange seriousness and remains uneasy about the look in his eyes.

108.modern-en: Levin is in Moscow trying to time a meeting with Kitty without seeming to.

110.modern-en: Levin keeps up his Moscow rounds, looking for the right moment to call on the Shtcherbatskys.

112.modern-en: Levin calls at the Shtcherbatskys' and finds Kitty alone with the others away.

116.modern-en: Levin and Kitty meet at the Oblonskys' party and stay near each other all evening.

125.modern-en: Levin spends his pre-wedding day in a haze of anxiety, half convinced Kitty will not turn up.

126.modern-en: Levin waits at the altar for what feels like a lifetime before Kitty arrives.

127.modern-en: Levin stands through the ceremony, only half hearing the priest.

128.modern-en: Levin marries Kitty in the long Orthodox ceremony.

129.modern-en: Levin leaves the wedding with Kitty for the country.

130.modern-en: Levin and Kitty begin married life at Pokrovskoe, with all the small shocks of two strangers sharing a house.

138.modern-en: Levin watches Kitty rearrange Pokrovskoe and is surprised to find that family life is not what he had imagined.

139.modern-en: Levin tries to get back into his book on agriculture while Kitty sews near him in the study.

140.modern-en: Levin reads the letter from Marya Nikolaevna saying Nikolay is dying and decides to go to him at once.

141.modern-en: Levin arrives at the provincial hotel with Kitty and finds Nikolay in a foul room, near death.

142.modern-en: Levin watches Kitty take over Nikolay's care and learns from her how to handle a dying man.

143.modern-en: Levin reflects on the gap between his intellectual fear of death and Kitty's quiet certainty about it.

144.modern-en: Levin is at his brother Nikolay's deathbed and sees him through extreme unction and the end.

158.modern-en: Levin is back at Pokrovskoe and welcomes Sergey Ivanovitch, Dolly, and the season's guests.

159.modern-en: Levin watches Sergey Ivanovitch with Varenka and hopes for a match without saying so.

160.modern-en: Levin works the estate while the women plan the mushroom expedition.

162.modern-en: Levin notices Sergey Ivanovitch's silence after the mushroom-picking and guesses what has not happened.

163.modern-en: Levin is host to the Pokrovskoe house party and watches everyone with new married eyes.

164.modern-en: Levin sees Varenka off and is left, like everyone else, slightly disappointed for Sergey Ivanovitch.

165.modern-en: Levin sets out with Stiva and Veslovsky for the long-planned snipe shooting.

166.modern-en: Levin has a bad day in the marsh: he misses easy shots and grows hot and out of temper.

167.modern-en: Levin keeps shooting badly and grumbles about Veslovsky's noise and luck.

168.modern-en: Levin watches Stiva and Veslovsky eat and drink among the peasants and feels both apart and at home.

169.modern-en: Levin sleeps the night in a peasant hut with his companions and lies awake thinking about Kitty.

171.modern-en: Levin is named in Dolly's thoughts on the way to Vozdvizhenskoe as the example of an enviable husband.

172.modern-en: Levin is referred to at Vozdvizhenskoe in passing in Anna and Dolly's conversation.

173.modern-en: Levin is invoked again in Dolly's thoughts about the gap between her sister Kitty's marriage and Anna's.

179.modern-en: Levin is mentioned as Dolly's brother-in-law as she travels back from Vozdvizhenskoe.

181.modern-en: Levin spends the late summer days at Pokrovskoe writing and waiting for the harvest to finish.

182.modern-en: Levin is dragged off by Sviazhsky to the provincial elections and reluctantly takes his seat.

183.modern-en: Levin sits through the long elections, baffled and irritated by the procedural battles.

184.modern-en: Levin tries, half against his will, to understand the marshal-of-the-nobility contest.

185.modern-en: Levin watches Nevyedovsky win the vote and is surprised by how much he cares.

186.modern-en: Levin is at the after-election celebrations and finds himself enjoying the company.

187.modern-en: Levin keeps up with the election dinners and decides he must go home to Kitty before too long.

190.modern-en: Levin arrives in Moscow with Kitty for the winter season, near her due date.

191.modern-en: Levin is unsettled by the pace of Moscow and his lack of useful work in the city.

192.modern-en: Levin goes the rounds of Moscow, paying visits and avoiding any of the salons he can avoid.

193.modern-en: Levin meets Metrov and others in the Moscow scientific world to discuss his book on agriculture.

194.modern-en: Levin attends a concert with Pestsov and listens to a piece on King Lear and Cordelia.

228.modern-en: Levin endures Sergey Ivanovitch and Katavasov's prodding about the Slav war.

230.modern-en: Levin spends the summer days walking the estate and reading on philosophy and faith.

41.modern-en: Kitty is mentioned in Petersburg circles as the girl whose engagement to Vronsky never happened.

48.modern-en: Kitty is referred to in passing at Pokrovskoe as the girl Levin lost.

2.modern-en: Dolly refuses to come down to breakfast and sends Matvey back with the message that she is leaving.

4.modern-en: Dolly receives Stiva's clumsy apology in her dressing room and breaks down again at the sight of him.

6.modern-en: Dolly is mentioned in Levin's brief account of why he is in Moscow.

9.modern-en: Dolly's drawing-room is the scene Levin remembers as he reflects on his old admiration for the Shtcherbatsky household.

12.modern-en: Dolly is named again as the older sister in the conversation about Kitty's prospects.

15.modern-en: Dolly is at her parents' house when Levin calls and is gentle with him over his hopes for Kitty.

19.modern-en: Dolly receives Anna in her bedroom; Anna takes her side against Stiva and starts to broker peace.

20.modern-en: Dolly listens to Anna's pleas for Stiva and slowly lets herself be persuaded into a reconciliation.

21.modern-en: Dolly finally lets Stiva back into her bed and quietly forgives him, thanks to Anna's intervention.

28.modern-en: Dolly is mentioned as the wife Stiva has just narrowly held onto, against her own better judgement.

32.modern-en: Dolly is referred to in passing as Anna's reluctant sister-in-law back in Moscow.

33.modern-en: Dolly is recalled in conversation as the elder sister who advised against trusting Vronsky.

36.modern-en: Dolly is named again as the older sister whose example haunts Kitty's first season.

37.modern-en: Dolly is mentioned by Kitty's mother as the cautionary case in their conversation about Kitty's choices.

69.modern-en: Dolly is named in passing as Stiva's wife as the family disperses for the summer.

75.modern-en: Dolly has taken the children to the country place at Ergushovo while Stiva stays in town.

76.modern-en: Dolly struggles with the run-down country house, the leaky roof, and the difficulty of feeding seven children.

77.modern-en: Dolly takes the children to a country church on Sunday and counts how thinly her resources stretch.

78.modern-en: Dolly visits Levin at Pokrovskoe and is welcomed warmly; Levin notices how worn she has grown.

79.modern-en: Dolly enjoys a quiet afternoon at Pokrovskoe and reflects on the difference between Levin's life and her own.

93.modern-en: Dolly is named again as Stiva's wife who has stayed on at Ergushovo with the children.

98.modern-en: Dolly is referred to in Levin's correspondence as the sister-in-law Kitty most wants to write to.

107.modern-en: Dolly hears the Petersburg news of Anna's near-fatal childbirth and Karenin's strange forgiveness.

108.modern-en: Dolly travels to Petersburg to support Anna and to see Seryozha if she can.

110.modern-en: Dolly stays with the Karenins and observes Karenin's stiff household in operation.

111.modern-en: Dolly pleads with Karenin to grant Anna her divorce so she may marry Vronsky.

112.modern-en: Dolly notes the changed Karenin and the half-broken Anna in the same household.

113.modern-en: Dolly continues to argue for Anna's right to a divorce, meeting Karenin's polite walls.

114.modern-en: Dolly is moved by Anna and pained by Karenin in equal measure.

115.modern-en: Dolly returns from Petersburg with little hope but with a deeper sympathy for Anna.

118.modern-en: Dolly is invoked in Vronsky's correspondence with Stiva as someone Anna would like to see.

123.modern-en: Dolly is in Moscow with the children for the Levin–Kitty wedding.

125.modern-en: Dolly helps Kitty get dressed on the wedding morning.

126.modern-en: Dolly is in the church for the ceremony and weeps quietly through it.

128.modern-en: Dolly stands among the women in the church and watches her younger sister marry.

129.modern-en: Dolly sees Kitty and Levin off after the wedding.

138.modern-en: Dolly is named again as the older sister Kitty most wants to invite to Pokrovskoe.

140.modern-en: Dolly is named in the letter from her that Kitty reads to Levin at the table.

158.modern-en: Dolly is invited by Anna to come to Vozdvizhenskoe and resolves to make the trip on Anna's account.

159.modern-en: Dolly is named among the visitors Pokrovskoe is preparing to receive.

163.modern-en: Dolly stays close to Kitty during the days at Pokrovskoe before her drive to see Anna.

164.modern-en: Dolly is named as the sister who will set out the next morning to Vozdvizhenskoe.

171.modern-en: Dolly drives across the country in a hired carriage on her way to Anna, brooding about Stiva and her own marriage.

172.modern-en: Dolly arrives at Vozdvizhenskoe and is met with practised hospitality by Vronsky and Anna.

173.modern-en: Dolly is shown the house, the new hospital, and the daughter Annie.

174.modern-en: Dolly watches Vronsky's circle of guests at dinner and notices the strain under Anna's good cheer.

175.modern-en: Dolly walks with Anna in the garden as Anna confides what she has lost and what she fears.

176.modern-en: Dolly is brought to see Vronsky's new model hospital and listens politely to his estate plans.

177.modern-en: Dolly sees through the Vozdvizhenskoe theatre and resolves she could not live this way.

178.modern-en: Dolly talks frankly with Anna about Seryozha and the divorce question and senses Anna's despair.

179.modern-en: Dolly takes her leave of Anna and Vronsky and is more relieved to go than she will admit.

180.modern-en: Dolly drives back home thinking of her own marriage with new tolerance after seeing Anna's.

181.modern-en: Dolly's visit is referred to in the Vozdvizhenskoe household as a small, mostly unhelpful event.

188.modern-en: Dolly is mentioned as the relative Kitty is most eager to invite to Pokrovskoe.

190.modern-en: Dolly is in Moscow with the children as Kitty and Levin arrive for the winter.

191.modern-en: Dolly receives Kitty and Levin and helps them settle into the city.

198.modern-en: Dolly is one of the women at the family gathering at the Princess's house in Moscow.

199.modern-en: Dolly is named in passing as Stiva's wife at the family gatherings in Moscow.

200.modern-en: Dolly is at home with the children when Stiva returns from his rounds.

202.modern-en: Dolly is among the women called in when Kitty goes into labour.

203.modern-en: Dolly assists at Kitty's labour through the night.

204.modern-en: Dolly is the one who tells Levin the baby has been born.

206.modern-en: Dolly is referred to as Stiva's wife back in Moscow as he goes to Petersburg about the divorce.

213.modern-en: Dolly is reported as having received Anna kindly during Anna's visit.

216.modern-en: Dolly's house is the place Anna calls at after her unsuccessful visit to Seryozha.

217.modern-en: Dolly receives Anna in the drawing room; Kitty is also there, and the encounter is awkward.

218.modern-en: Dolly sees Anna off after the brief visit and is left uneasy about her state.

226.modern-en: Dolly stays at Pokrovskoe with her sister Kitty and her children during the summer.

227.modern-en: Dolly enjoys the country evenings at Pokrovskoe and watches Levin's restlessness from a distance.

233.modern-en: Dolly is mentioned as one of the women in the Pokrovskoe household.

234.modern-en: Dolly is at dinner during Sergey Ivanovitch and Katavasov's debate on the Slavic war.

235.modern-en: Dolly is in the house and out in the garden as the long summer days continue.

236.modern-en: Dolly is named again at the family dinner table during the political discussion.

237.modern-en: Dolly is among the household scrambling to bring the children inside when the storm breaks.

5.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is named as Levin's celebrated half-brother, the famous Moscow writer.

24.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is invoked by Nikolay Levin in his drunken outburst as the brother he most resents.

25.modern-en: Levin reflects on how unreachable Nikolay is to Sergey Ivanovitch's calm rationalism.

48.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is mentioned as the brother whose calm Levin envies during the spring at Pokrovskoe.

71.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch watches Levin set off to mow with the peasants and gently mocks the idea.

73.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch keeps to his work and his fishing while Levin throws himself back into the harvest.

75.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch teases Levin about how poorly he keeps up his end of a serious conversation.

100.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is in residence at Pokrovskoe when Nikolay arrives unannounced and skeletal.

107.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is mentioned in Petersburg society as a public figure on the question of the Slav cause.

108.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch's writings are discussed in the same Petersburg circles that whisper about Anna.

110.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch's books are taken up in connection with the growing public mood over the Slav question.

111.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is referred to in passing in Karenin's circle as a writer to keep an eye on.

113.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is mentioned in the conversation Stiva has with Levin about the family's affairs.

115.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch's career is invoked as Levin tries to explain his own to a sceptical landowner.

125.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch comes to Moscow for Levin's wedding to Kitty.

126.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch stands by Levin as best man before the ceremony begins.

128.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is one of the witnesses at the church for Levin and Kitty's wedding.

129.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch toasts the couple at the small wedding gathering before they depart for the country.

144.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch's name is brought up at Nikolay Levin's deathbed as the brother who could not bear to come.

158.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch returns to Pokrovskoe for the summer and is met by his sister-in-law Kitty.

160.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch walks in the garden with Varenka and acknowledges that he is drawn to her.

162.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch hears the moment slip past him as he and Varenka talk about birch boletes instead.

164.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch takes his leave of Pokrovskoe shortly after Varenka does.

173.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is mentioned among the public men still talking about the Slav question.

182.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch joins Levin at the provincial elections and works for the modernising party.

183.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch lobbies among the gentry for Nevyedovsky's election.

184.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch advises Levin behind the scenes during the marshal-of-the-nobility ballot.

185.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch celebrates Nevyedovsky's victory as a step for the cause.

186.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch keeps Levin close during the after-election dinners.

187.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch's public confidence after the elections begins to wear on Levin.

196.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is at the English Club with Levin and Stiva, working a different room of the gentry.

197.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch's name is dropped repeatedly in the club's political conversations.

224.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch sees Vronsky off at the station, headed for Serbia after Anna's death.

229.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch tries to draw Levin into a public-spirited discussion of the Serbian volunteers.

230.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch joins the household excursions and treats his brother's questions with affectionate patience.

237.modern-en: Sergey Ivanovitch is among the company when the great summer thunderstorm breaks over Pokrovskoe.

11.modern-en: The thought of his brother Nikolay returns to torment Levin again as Oblonsky tells him about Vronsky as a rival.

24.modern-en: Walking to his brother's lodgings, Levin recalls Nikolay's whole history of debauchery and scandals, then finds him in cheap rooms with Kritsky and Marya Nikolaevna.

25.modern-en: Nikolay rants to Konstantin about his locksmiths' association and Sergey Ivanovitch, drinks himself stupid, and Konstantin gets him to bed hopelessly drunk.

19.modern-en: Anna's love for her son Seryozha is what she names first when she defends her marriage to Dolly.

61.modern-en: Seryozha is brought to say goodnight to Anna on the evening of the steeplechase.

84.modern-en: Seryozha is mentioned as the one tie binding Anna to her old life as she contemplates leaving Karenin.

105.modern-en: Seryozha is told by Karenin that his mother is ill, then increasingly that she is no longer to be spoken of.

118.modern-en: Seryozha is mentioned as the child Anna has lost and longs to see again from Italy.

124.modern-en: Seryozha is reported as growing thin and quiet under Lidia Ivanovna's regime.

181.modern-en: Seryozha is mentioned as the child Anna keeps writing to without reply.

208.modern-en: Anna's longing for Seryozha returns sharply as her position with Vronsky weakens.

212.modern-en: Seryozha is named again as the loss Anna cannot get over.

219.modern-en: Seryozha is among Anna's last thoughts as she travels to the station that will be her end.

222.modern-en: Lidia Ivanovna is briefly named as Karenin's continuing companion after Anna's death.

235.modern-en: Lidia Ivanovna remains at Karenin's side in his retreat from public life.

epithet.en: Petersburg society hostess who covers for Anna's affair, then drops her
epithet.da: Petersborgs selskabsdame, der dækker over Annas affære og siden vender hende ryggen

33.modern-en: Betsy Tverskaya is introduced as the queen of Petersburg's smart, lightly indecent set; Anna and Vronsky meet at her drawing rooms.

34.modern-en: Betsy stages a soirée at which Anna and Vronsky talk apart in plain view of the whole room.

38.modern-en: Betsy steers the conversation around Anna's behaviour with her usual breezy worldliness.

39.modern-en: Betsy plays hostess for the set that has tacitly licensed the affair as long as appearances hold.

40.modern-en: Betsy ushers Anna to a corner with Vronsky and keeps the rest of the room politely facing away.

41.modern-en: Betsy assures Anna that nothing is amiss as long as she observes the forms; Karenin's house is mentioned only obliquely.

44.modern-en: Betsy is named in passing as the embodiment of the Petersburg social code Anna is starting to chafe at.

53.modern-en: Betsy's name comes up in Vronsky's regiment circle as the woman who has Anna under her wing.

56.modern-en: Betsy is mentioned as the friend Anna sees most often in Petersburg.

57.modern-en: Betsy carries on her usual programme of receptions even as the strain at the Karenins' grows.

58.modern-en: Betsy is at the steeplechase, watching Anna watch Vronsky.

60.modern-en: Betsy is described as the leading figure of the worldly clique Karenin's pious circle dislikes.

61.modern-en: Betsy continues to host Anna in defiance of growing Petersburg disapproval.

62.modern-en: Betsy's drawing room remains one of the few places Anna can still appear in society.

63.modern-en: Betsy is one of the few to come to Anna while her illness keeps her at home.

84.modern-en: Betsy is mentioned as the one woman whose acquaintance Anna has not lost during the scandal.

85.modern-en: Betsy passes along the latest reports of Anna and Vronsky to her circle.

86.modern-en: Betsy hovers near Karenin's household to register what is being said and unsaid.

87.modern-en: Betsy carries the news of Anna's worsening situation back through the Petersburg salons.

90.modern-en: Betsy is named again as the one society figure who has stayed close to Anna and Vronsky.

91.modern-en: Betsy's set continues to receive Anna, though Anna increasingly senses what the smiles cost.

107.modern-en: Betsy's reception is the public test Anna fails, when ladies turn their backs at the opera box.

120.modern-en: Betsy is mentioned in conversation between Dolly and Anna as someone Anna no longer sees.

121.modern-en: Betsy is invoked as one of the women whose friendship has cooled now that Anna has stopped hiding.

122.modern-en: Betsy is mentioned again as part of the Petersburg world that has quietly closed around Anna.

124.modern-en: Betsy's social cover, once enough to keep Anna in the world, has run out.

145.modern-en: Betsy is referred to in the conversation about who will and will not receive Anna now.

152.modern-en: Betsy is named again as Anna's last society contact, increasingly noncommittal.

156.modern-en: Betsy is mentioned as one of the women who let it be known they would not come to Anna's box at the opera.

176.modern-en: Betsy comes up again when Dolly asks Anna who from the old set she still hears from.

180.modern-en: Betsy is named in passing as a Petersburg figure Anna and Vronsky still see from time to time.

209.modern-en: Betsy is mentioned among the names in Karenin's pious circle's running tally of Anna's losses.

211.modern-en: Betsy turns up in Stiva's account of the people still in some kind of contact with Anna.

epithet.en: Madame Stahl's pious companion, befriended by Kitty at the spa
epithet.da: Madame Stahls fromme ledsagerske, som Kitty bliver veninde med ved kurbadet

64.modern-en: At Soden spa, Kitty notices the pious young woman who walks the gardens caring for the sick and learns her name is Varenka.

65.modern-en: Kitty finally meets Varenka and is at once drawn to her air of dignified self-sacrifice.

66.modern-en: Varenka takes Kitty along to see the bedridden painter Petrov; Kitty watches Varenka work with the sick and decides to model herself on her.

67.modern-en: Varenka tells Kitty the story of Madame Stahl and her own foundling history, and gives Kitty a glimpse of her quiet inner life.

68.modern-en: Varenka deflects Kitty's gushing admiration with calm humility as Kitty tries to throw herself into the same work.

69.modern-en: Kitty parts from Varenka and Madame Stahl at Soden, having learned from Varenka that her piety cannot be borrowed and must be her own.

112.modern-en: Varenka is mentioned in passing as a former Soden acquaintance whom Kitty still admires.

158.modern-en: Varenka arrives at Pokrovskoe to visit Kitty, who is hoping to set her up with Sergey Ivanovitch.

159.modern-en: Varenka helps Agafea Mihalovna with the jam-making and charms the Pokrovskoe household with her composure.

160.modern-en: Walking in the garden with Sergey Ivanovitch, Varenka senses his interest but stays carefully serene.

161.modern-en: Out picking mushrooms, Varenka waits for Sergey Ivanovitch to propose; he can almost manage it but turns the talk to mushrooms instead.

162.modern-en: Varenka returns from the woods understanding that the moment has passed and Sergey Ivanovitch will not speak.

163.modern-en: Varenka stays on at Pokrovskoe a little longer, gently steering conversations away from her near-engagement.

164.modern-en: Varenka takes her leave of Pokrovskoe and Kitty, knowing the match with Sergey Ivanovitch will not happen.

172.modern-en: Varenka is recalled when Sergey Ivanovitch and Dolly discuss the recent visit to Pokrovskoe.

173.modern-en: Varenka is mentioned again as someone Sergey Ivanovitch chose, in the end, not to marry.

26.modern-en: Levin comes home crushed from Moscow; Agafea Mihalovna has his rooms warmed and his supper laid out as if nothing has changed.

27.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna fusses over Levin's meals and listens to his half-spoken misery without commenting on it.

46.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna oversees the bee yard and the spring cleaning as Levin throws himself back into the estate.

48.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna mentions to Levin that his brother Nikolay has been ill, prompting Levin's letter to Moscow.

51.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna keeps the household running while Levin loses himself in farm work to forget Kitty.

71.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna fixes Levin a meal of curd and cream and bread when he returns from the early-morning mowing.

72.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna shakes her head over Levin's plan to mow with the peasants but sees to it that he is fed.

75.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna sits with Levin while he writes by lamplight after a long day in the meadows.

99.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna is the first to register that Levin's brother Nikolay has returned, mortally ill.

100.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna prepares Nikolay's room and tends to him with the same quiet competence she gives Levin.

138.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna takes the loss of her keys to the young mistress Kitty hard, but is slowly won over by her.

140.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna sits with Kitty over tea, and Kitty handles her with a tact that finally smooths the household over.

143.modern-en: Levin reflects that Agafea Mihalovna and Kitty both know how to handle the dying Nikolay with a certainty intellectual men cannot match.

159.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna and Varenka boil jam together; Agafea Mihalovna defends her recipes against Kitty's reforms.

163.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna shares her quiet judgments with Kitty about the Pokrovskoe guests, especially Varenka.

164.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna makes up the house after Varenka and the visitors leave, restoring her usual order.

226.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna helps Kitty with baby Mitya and offers Levin her old-woman's reassurance that the boy will be fine.

227.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna brings tea to Levin as he wrestles with his religious questions in the study.

237.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna calmly takes charge during the storm, helping Kitty get the baby to safety.

238.modern-en: Agafea Mihalovna's small remark about a peasant living for God comes back to Levin as part of his quiet conversion.

epithet.en: Levin's worldly neighbour, marshal of the local nobility
epithet.da: Levins verdsligt orienterede nabo, marskal for den lokale adel

93.modern-en: Levin sets out for Sviazhsky's estate to look at his model farm and to escape his own restlessness.

94.modern-en: Sviazhsky welcomes Levin warmly, surrounded by his sister, his wife, and a houseful of other liberal landowners.

95.modern-en: Sviazhsky chairs an after-dinner debate on the future of Russian agriculture and refuses to commit to any conclusion of his own.

96.modern-en: Sviazhsky pushes Levin to articulate his ideas but never reveals his own underlying view.

97.modern-en: Sviazhsky's hospitality continues; Levin notices the gap between his liberal opinions and his settled domestic life.

98.modern-en: Sviazhsky's smooth refusal to take Levin's questions seriously gives Levin the idea for his own farm-labour scheme.

115.modern-en: Sviazhsky is mentioned in passing as one of the provincial figures Levin still owes a visit.

117.modern-en: Sviazhsky's name comes up among the landowners Levin keeps in contact with about agriculture.

125.modern-en: Sviazhsky is named again as a neighbour Levin sees during the rounds of the summer.

173.modern-en: Sviazhsky reappears in Part 6 as a guest passing through the country estates near Vronsky and Anna.

174.modern-en: Sviazhsky drives over with Veslovsky and Stiva for the snipe shooting at the marsh.

176.modern-en: Sviazhsky stays on at the shooting party and joins the conversations about local politics.

177.modern-en: Sviazhsky discusses the provincial elections that are about to be held and presses Levin to come.

178.modern-en: Sviazhsky brings up Anna's situation indirectly as part of his sketch of the changing country society.

179.modern-en: Sviazhsky departs the shooting party and arranges to meet Levin again at the election.

182.modern-en: Sviazhsky is at the provincial elections, working the room with his usual lightness.

183.modern-en: Sviazhsky maneuvers among the rival factions, pulling Levin into the modernising party's ranks.

184.modern-en: Sviazhsky explains the procedural fight over the marshal of the nobility to the bewildered Levin.

185.modern-en: Sviazhsky helps engineer Nevyedovsky's election over the old marshal Snetkov.

186.modern-en: Sviazhsky takes Levin around after the vote, introducing him to the new wave of provincial men.

187.modern-en: Sviazhsky's faction celebrates the victory; Sviazhsky himself stays smooth and amused as ever.

188.modern-en: Sviazhsky takes his leave of Levin at the end of the elections, both of them tired and pleased.

195.modern-en: Sviazhsky is mentioned among the men Levin runs into in Moscow after the election.

196.modern-en: Sviazhsky turns up at the English Club where Levin has come with Stiva.

197.modern-en: Sviazhsky takes Levin through the club's rooms and introduces him to more Moscow figures.

epithet.en: Vronsky's regiment friend, a heavy gambler and drinker

53.modern-en: Captain Yashvin enters the regiment dining room; Vronsky calls him his closest friend and the strongest character in the regiment.

54.modern-en: Yashvin barges into Petritsky's room with Vronsky and tugs the rug off him to drag him out of bed.

59.modern-en: After Vronsky's catastrophic fall at the steeplechase, Yashvin catches up to him with his cap and walks him home.

88.modern-en: Yashvin and Venovsky cover Vronsky's gambling debt back when Vronsky hadn't even been playing.

90.modern-en: Yashvin lounges in Vronsky's quarters when Serpuhovskoy arrives, and the colonel asks him to keep an eye on Vronsky.

91.modern-en: Vronsky borrows Yashvin's hired fly so he can drive across town to Anna's without his own horses being recognized.

155.modern-en: Yashvin turns up at Vronsky's place in Petersburg; when Vronsky comes to Anna, he brings Yashvin with him instead of coming alone.

156.modern-en: Yashvin stays for dinner with Anna and Vronsky, then goes off to smoke as Anna's mood turns dangerously bright.

157.modern-en: Yashvin sits with Vronsky drinking brandy and seltzer, recommends a horse, and heads to the opera while Anna goes there alone.

196.modern-en: At the club Vronsky points out Yashvin to Turovtsin, holding court at a crowded card table.

197.modern-en: Stiva finds Yashvin losing badly in the club's "infernal regions" and stays back to watch over his play.

201.modern-en: Vronsky sends word through Stiva that he can't leave Yashvin, who is at one point up seventeen thousand at cards.

214.modern-en: Yashvin walks in on Vronsky and Anna mid-quarrel; Anna asks him pointedly whether his debt has been paid.

218.modern-en: Riding through Moscow, Anna remembers Yashvin's line that one man wants to strip the other of his shirt and the other wants the same.

219.modern-en: Yashvin's belief that the struggle for existence and hatred are the one thing holding people together comes back to Anna near the end.

224.modern-en: Yashvin, who has lost everything at cards, joins Vronsky on the train heading to the Serbian war after Anna's death.
